A_target.statement:
Let $G$ be a [[Definition:Graph (Graph Theory)|graph]].
Then $G$ is [[Definition:Bipartite Graph|bipartite]] {{iff}} $G$ contains no [[Definition:Cycle (Graph Theory)|cycle]] of [[Definition:Odd Integer|odd]] length.

B_source.statement: A [[Definition:Graph (Graph Theory)|graph]] $G$ is [[Definition:K-Colorable Graph|$2$-colorable]] {{iff}} there exists a [[Definition:Proper Vertex Coloring|proper vertex coloring]] of $G$ with $2$ colors.

validity_conditions: Bipartite and 2-colorable are literally the same property: a bipartition IS a proper 2-coloring, with parts as color classes.
The odd-cycle characterization then follows because a 2-coloring propagated along a path forces the parity of any returning cycle to be even.
proof_plan: A [[Definition:Bipartition|bipartition]] $\tuple {L, R}$ of $G$ is the same as a proper $2$-coloring: color the [[Definition:Vertex of Graph|vertices]] of $L$ with one color and those of $R$ with the other.

In each [[Definition:Connected Graph|component]], fix a root and color vertices by the parity of their distance from it, as in [[Definition:Breadth-First Search|breadth-first search]].
A proper $2$-coloring exists {{iff}} this propagation never assigns the same color to both ends of an [[Definition:Edge of Graph|edge]].

A conflict on an edge $u v$ with $\map d u \equiv \map d v \pmod 2$ closes a cycle of length $\map d u + \map d v + 1$, which is [[Definition:Odd Integer|odd]].
Conversely, an odd cycle cannot be properly $2$-colored, since colors must alternate around it.

Hence $G$ is [[Definition:Bipartite Graph|bipartite]] {{iff}} $G$ has no [[Definition:Odd Integer|odd]] [[Definition:Cycle (Graph Theory)|cycle]].
{{qed}}
